"Google controlled all of advertising. Every single person googled everything. They had a monopoly on attention when it came to the Internet. You had to go through the Google page to do anything."

tweets.text:
Alphabet $GOOGL shares down over 8% after-hours despite a doubling in cloud revenues as nearly everything else misses and free cash flow goes negative. 

▪️ Revenue: $127.6 billion (+24.7% year over year) vs. $128.2 billion estimate
▪️ Earnings per share: $2.12 vs. $3.02 estimate.
▪️Mark-to-market whiplash: other income swung from a $98.0 billion gain in Q2, mostly gains on equity holdings that added $6.26 to earnings per share, to an $8.2 billion loss in Q3. That’s a roughly $106 billion turnaround, and net income fell from $112.2 billion in Q2 to $26.5 billion. Adding the loss back gets you about $2.67, still an 11.6% miss
▪️ Cloud: $30.7 billion (+103% year over year) vs. $29.15 billion estimate; operating income $11.1 billion vs. $9.75 billion, a 36.2% margin
▪️ Search: $63.4 billion vs. $65.0 billion estimate; YouTube ads $11.2 billion vs. $11.4 billion; subscriptions $14.3 billion vs. $14.85 billion
▪️ Operating income: $40.6 billion vs. $43.2 billion estimate
▪️ Capex: $51.4 billion, about 40% of revenue and more than double the $24.0 billion a year ago (TipRanks)
▪️ Free cash flow: −$9.1 billion vs. −$2.7 billion estimate; zero buybacks

One for the bulls: Cloud’s operating-income beat (+13.8%) was the largest of any line item. Cloud is now about 24% of revenue, and Pichai cited strong demand for TPU systems “across a wide range of customers.” Token processing on first-party model APIs is more than four times what it was a year ago. Operating income still grew 30% year over year, faster than revenue’s 24.7%, even with research and development spending up 36% to $20.6 billion (TipRanks).

One for the bears: The cash miss wasn’t a spending problem. Capex actually came in $3.8 billion under estimates. Operating cash flow fell $10.4 billion (20%) short, even though operating income missed by only 6%. That gap between earnings and cash is something to listen for on the call.

Consensus figures as compiled by Wall St Engine; earnings-per-share estimate from LSEG via CNBC.

tweets.full_text:
Alphabet $GOOGL shares down over 8% after-hours despite a doubling in cloud revenues as nearly everything else misses and free cash flow goes negative. 

▪️ Revenue: $127.6 billion (+24.7% year over year) vs. $128.2 billion estimate
▪️ Earnings per share: $2.12 vs. $3.02 estimate.
▪️Mark-to-market whiplash: other income swung from a $98.0 billion gain in Q2, mostly gains on equity holdings that added $6.26 to earnings per share, to an $8.2 billion loss in Q3. That’s a roughly $106 billion turnaround, and net income fell from $112.2 billion in Q2 to $26.5 billion. Adding the loss back gets you about $2.67, still an 11.6% miss
▪️ Cloud: $30.7 billion (+103% year over year) vs. $29.15 billion estimate; operating income $11.1 billion vs. $9.75 billion, a 36.2% margin
▪️ Search: $63.4 billion vs. $65.0 billion estimate; YouTube ads $11.2 billion vs. $11.4 billion; subscriptions $14.3 billion vs. $14.85 billion
▪️ Operating income: $40.6 billion vs. $43.2 billion estimate
▪️ Capex: $51.4 billion, about 40% of revenue and more than double the $24.0 billion a year ago (TipRanks)
▪️ Free cash flow: −$9.1 billion vs. −$2.7 billion estimate; zero buybacks

One for the bulls: Cloud’s operating-income beat (+13.8%) was the largest of any line item. Cloud is now about 24% of revenue, and Pichai cited strong demand for TPU systems “across a wide range of customers.” Token processing on first-party model APIs is more than four times what it was a year ago. Operating income still grew 30% year over year, faster than revenue’s 24.7%, even with research and development spending up 36% to $20.6 billion (TipRanks).

One for the bears: The cash miss wasn’t a spending problem. Capex actually came in $3.8 billion under estimates. Operating cash flow fell $10.4 billion (20%) short, even though operating income missed by only 6%. That gap between earnings and cash is something to listen for on the call.

Consensus figures as compiled by Wall St Engine; earnings-per-share estimate from LSEG via CNBC.

tweets.text:
Demand is becoming a bigger driver of US inflation:

Demand-driven components contributed +1.2 percentage points to the +3.4% YoY increase in PCE inflation in August, the largest contribution since September 2023.

At the same time, supply-driven factors added +1.0 percentage point, while ambiguous factors accounted for another +1.2 percentage points.

This contrasts with the post-pandemic inflation surge, when supply disruptions were the main driver.

In 2022, supply-driven components contributed an average of +3.1 percentage points per month to headline PCE inflation, compared with +2.6 percentage points per month from demand-driven factors.

This is a key distinction for Fed policy, as rising interest rates can slow demand, while their impact on supply-side pressures is limited.

The composition of US inflation is shifting.

Mark Cuban's advice for young people boils down to "there's gonna be two types of companies: those who are great at AI and those who have gone out of business."

"And then there's two types of people in how they use AI: those who use AI to learn anything, and those who use AI so they don't have to learn anything."

"And if you're one of those people who uses AI so that you can learn anything, and you realize what type of companies and problems aren't being solved by AI, don't be shy to just talk to your AI."

"And I say this not just to kids, but to 50 60, 70-year-old entrepreneurs. The biggest challenge right now with entrepreneurs using AI is the comfort level of talking to your AI... there's still a lot of hesitancy."

"Just like back in the day, those first spreadsheets, people still had their 10-key adding machine, and they would check it to make sure the spreadsheets were right."

"So when you ask me, is there one thing I truly believe, it's everything. Everything will change. This is the greatest transitional technology we have ever seen, and I've been around for all of them, right? This blows them all away."

@mcuban @julesyoo @eriktorenberg

This is where tokenized stocks start to get interesting

@0xbeans proposes splitting one tokenized share into two tradable tokens: 

1) one capturing overnight price moves
2) the other regular trading session moves

A similar idea to Pendle splitting principal and yield, applied to WHEN a stock generates its returns

The two windows can behave very differently, so separating them could let investors trade overnight earnings exposure, hedge specific periods and build DeFi strategies around either leg

Both tokens together remain redeemable for the underlying share

Still an early proposal, but a useful example of how programmable stocks could create entirely new markets around familiar assets

We’ve already seen a plethora of value accrue to STANDARD charter holders, I’d hazard a guess there’s a lot more to come

We’re still in the early innings of what’s possible with tokenized stocks, and if you believe Robinhood will be the leader then there’s some pretty clear winners emerging that are worth tracking closely

In a single year, AI has rewritten the security priority list for CISOs.

Attackers are moving faster. Bain estimates AI compresses a typical cyberattack from about four weeks to about 18 hours, and models keep getting better at finding and exploiting weaknesses.

There's also more to protect, with employees shipping apps they couldn't have built a year ago and agents getting access to source code, documents, and production systems.

In a survey of 100 CISOs at companies with 1,000+ employees, all seven of the most-selected 2027 priorities involve AI.

The biggest jumps since 2026:
- Internal AI agent security (+28 pts)
- AI SOC (+26 pts)
- AI offensive security (+24 pts)
- AI code security (+23 pts)
- AI vulnerability remediation (+22 pts)

Last year's staples:
- Exposure & vulnerability management (-21 pts)
- SIEM / security data (-18 pts)
- Privileged access management (-18 pts)

From a16z's @OwenColby and @steph_zhang on The New Security Agenda: https://t.co/C814PJ4wGg

tweets.text:
a16z's Martin Casado says many debates about VC turn into "a muddled, incoherent mess" because investors pull arguments from four investing mindsets that often conflict:

1. Financial: the business's finances are the asset, so investors judge deals on metrics like churn, margin, and growth, plus the size of the market.

2. Productive: the tech is the asset, and it creates new markets, so investors focus on tech, team, and market fit, and treat today's TAM as secondary.

3. Frontier: the founders are the asset, so investors back the best team in a wildly new space well before anything is working.

4. Speculative: investors have little visibility into the company, so they bet on the market's perception of the deal, with a heavy focus on price and timing.

Each one is coherent on its own, but using them as a grab bag breaks down, because "it's hard to directly refute a finance argument with a product argument since they make entirely different assumptions on what the bet is for value creation."

Martin's answer is to pick one core philosophy as a team and stick to it across deals, or evolve it by stage: frontier before there's a product, productive before traction, and financial once the business is repeatable.

He's "strictly a productive investor" and thinks new tech tends to create its own market, like "Uber and taxis, GitHub and the repository, Cursor and the IDE."

In his words, "If you truly believe a technology is revolutionary, TAM concerns should be third order at best."

Full piece from Martin: https://t.co/F5JdvxqOkq

The disconnect between oil stocks and the broader market has rarely been wider:

The 6-month correlation between the S&P 500 Energy Sector and the S&P 500 is down to -0.38, near its lowest on record.

This marks a sharp reversal from a positive correlation of +0.74 observed in June 2025.

In the last week of September, this figure fell as low as -0.45, the lowest reading in data going back to the 1980s.

The only other time since the late 1980s when the correlation between these two indices turned negative was in 2000 and 2001, during the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

This all comes as the S&P 500 Energy Sector has rallied +23.1% over the last 6 months, significantly outperforming the S&P 500’s gain of +7.1%.

Energy stocks are having a historic year amid the Iran War.

Mark Cuban says the lack of AI adoption in organizations means the "trillionaire in the basement" entrepreneur is coming:

"You have to be able to understand as a CEO and in the C-suite how all those things impact your company. Once you get a good grasp on that... you can just find new ways for things to happen that benefit your customers or create new opportunities."

"And that's the brilliance of AI, right? AI is not smart. It's book smart maybe, but it's not street smart. It's not entrepreneur smart. You've got to have somebody there who guides it and helps it."

"But until you have a C-suite that understands how it works, it's gonna be very difficult for that organization."

"I literally sat with the head of a consumer food company... I'm like, 'Okay, well, let's do this. Let's take your number one product, your cookie, right? And I'm gonna ask ChatGPT to create a competitor...' And in about three minutes he was like, 'Oh, s**t.'"

"There's no better time to be an entrepreneur than right now. There will be the trillionaire in the basement."

@mcuban @eriktorenberg @julesyoo

BREAKING: The Consumer Confidence Index surged +7.5 points in October, to 91.7, its highest since May 2026.

This marks its largest monthly increase since May 2025.

The Present Situation Index jumped +8.6 points, to 120.4, its highest since April.

At the same time, the Expectations Index rose +6.9 points, to 72.6, nearly reversing 3 consecutive monthly declines.

The increase in sentiment was largely driven by the recent decline in retail gasoline prices, which provided some relief to household budgets.

Furthermore, consumers reported improved perceptions of the job market and business conditions.

Consumer confidence remains highly volatile.

Mark Cuban scaled Cost Plus Drugs from about 100 generics to roughly 4,000 at a flat 15% markup, forcing incumbents to change prices in ways decades of policy never did.

He thinks AI could transform healthcare, but it won't fix opaque prices and broken incentives on its own.

Mark sits down with a16z's Julie Yoo and Erik Torenberg to discuss what he's learned building Cost Plus Drugs, why trust is its core product, and how greater transparency could put pressure on healthcare costs.

They also explore why drugs designed for your DNA could cost close to nothing, the football field-sized drug plant his team shrank into tractor trailer-sized pods, his plan to make generics in Dallas for less than he pays manufacturers in India, and why every company will either be great at AI or go out of business.

Social Security's retirement trust fund hits zero in 2032. That is seven years away, not some distant abstraction.

Once the reserves run dry, the program can only pay what it collects, roughly 78% of promised benefits. That is an automatic 22% cut unless Congress acts. Combining the retirement and disability funds buys two years, to 2034, and still only covers about 83%.

Washington will patch it eventually, with higher payroll taxes, a later retirement age, or smaller checks. You cannot build a retirement around a coin flip in Congress. Build your own income stream now, and treat whatever Social Security pays as a bonus, not the plan.

Now the big money is moving in. Brookfield, J.P. Morgan and Starwood are all building portfolios. When Blackstone is financing dirt lots, the AI capex wave has reached the pick-and-shovel layer. The boom shows up in places nobody is looking.

Everyone is convinced the Fed is strangling the economy. The math says rates are actually kind of low.

The fed-funds rate sits near 3.75%. The New York Fed's model puts the neutral rate, the level that neither slows nor speeds the economy, at roughly 4%. Fed officials themselves peg the long-run rate near 3.2%. Either way, today's policy is barely restrictive, if at all.

This guts the easing story. The Fed is not sitting on a stack of cuts. Today's rate is close to normal, and that normal is higher than the last decade trained you to expect. Stop pricing in a return to zero.

#Uranium #Copper #Gold #Silver
⚒️ DAILY METALS PULS — OCTOBER 28 | POST-FED UPDATE
The Fed held rates at 3.75–4.00% in a 10–2 vote. Both dissenters wanted a 25-basis-point hike. With inflation still elevated and economic activity described as strong, my reading is a hawkish hold: further tightening remains a risk.

🥇 GOLD: Back above $4,070

Spot gold was $4,073.40/oz, up 0.35% on Kitco’s daily comparison, at 4:06 p.m. New York time.

That puts gold comfortably above the roughly $4,030 level quoted in the earlier update. Encouraging resilience following the decision, although one afternoon’s recovery needs follow-through.

🥈 SILVER: Recovers above $54

Spot silver was $54.43/oz, up 0.26%, around 4:04 p.m. New York time, after trading as low as $53.18 during the session.

The gold/silver ratio is approximately 74.8. Silver has recovered, but I’m watching whether it can reclaim $55 and sustain the move.

🟠 COPPER: Above $14,500

The LME’s latest published three-month closing price is $14,621/t. Its closing table also shows aluminium at $3,250/t and tin at $54,010/t.

Copper has moved above the $14,500 level highlighted earlier. These are LME closing benchmarks, established before the Fed announcement—not a measure of the post-decision reaction.

☢️ URANIUM: Contracting remains the signal

The latest verified industry briefing I’m using remains October 27: physical spot at $89.85/lb for the previous Friday and October’s long-term indicator at $97/lb.

Reported year-to-date term contracting stands at 80.4 million pounds versus 47.9 million a year earlier—approximately 68% higher. These are dated industry assessments, not live post-Fed quotes.

My take: gold and silver’s recovery is encouraging despite the Fed’s continued inflation concerns. Copper’s elevated pricing and stronger uranium contracting add separate reasons to keep watching the sector.

The next test is whether precious metals hold these gains as markets digest the decision and the next inflation data.

tweets.text:
This same phenomena is happening in physical AI

Even after GPT-4 came out, I remember talking to computer scientists/ML experts that were so confident that general purpose models were overhyped and wouldn’t be able to produce real useful work soon. A lot of reductionist talk about stochastic parrots and next token predictors. 

It is surprisingly difficult for a lot of career technologists to grasp non linear technological trends and how slopes can change. 

Different experts in the same domain can have widely different expectations for technological advancement even 1-2 years in the future. 

There is also an element of information asymmetry. Organizations on the frontier move at vastly different paces than those that don’t. They are privy to key know how and training/data collection approaches that can potentially compress R&D pace by orders of magnitude. 

It’s important to remember that those that aren’t on the frontier are somewhat blind to the full state of the world even though they might not think that they are.

We see time and time again that research paradigms are always changing and the same bottlenecks that existed yesterday get solved by smart brains (and AI models) motivated enough to tackle them.

Laggards claim “we are so far”. We bet on the people that respond with “skill issue”.

We're in the early stages of a multi year Mac super cycle. 

This morning, $AAPL announced some Mac updates, including 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac models (M6 chips). Still waiting on the first touchscreen Mac announcement later this morning.

Pricing is unchanged today. Keep in mind that late in June they raised the price of the MacBook by 18% and the iMac by 16%.

My take: There is upside to the Mac over the next two years. Mac has gone from 8.6% of revenue in June 2025 to 9.5% in June 2026. Last quarter it grew 29%. The Street is expecting 12% y/y in Sep ’26, going to 6% growth in FY27 and FY28.

Most important: I believe we are in the early stages of a multi-year AI-powered hardware upgrade cycle. Consumers and businesses will need to buy new hardware, even at higher prices, to fully leverage AI. That’s good for Mac growth. I expect FY27 Mac to grow above 10% (Street at 6%) and FY28 above 10% (Street at 6%).

ˢᵐᵃˡˡ ˢⁱᶻᵉ ᵈᵒᵉˢ ᵐᵃᵗᵗᵉʳ

There are two kinds of stocks where you should assume you have little or no alpha: companies with a market cap above $100 billion, followed by analysts everywhere, and stocks followed by everyone on X—especially ones being pushed by stock influencers with four-year track records.

Screaming that a company trades at a P/E of 16 isn’t an edge. Everyone has the numbers on their desk. Plenty of smart analysts are following these companies. You might still invest in them, but understand that you probably don’t have alpha just because you spotted a familiar metric.

I look for opportunities in $1–5 billion companies I know well. When a smaller company falls, there may be nobody waiting to buy. Only a few people follow it, and the big holders already own a lot. That can make selling unusually aggressive. $WGS fell 17% in one day, with no news and about three times normal volume. If I wanted out of a position like that, I’d spread the selling over a week. Why dump it all in one day at triple the volume? It looked like someone needed out fast.

Make a habit of knowing 12 companies very well. When one falls 15%, check for news or an earnings announcement, then use what you know about the business to judge whether something has really changed—or whether someone may be stuck and selling fast. That’s when you may find a dislocation worth acting on.

$WGS could have been bought around $55 a week ago. It’s back near $67 now. That’s the kind of opportunity I mean. A no-news drop can still signal a real problem, so you have to know what you own well enough to judge the difference.

If you don’t know what you own, you’ll probably panic when it drops, especially if you’re still in that dumb phase of buying things you don’t understand and underperforming the market because of it. Then you ask me, “What’s new?” If you think I have insider information, don’t ask. Everything I know is publicly available online. I don’t have inside information about any of these companies.

The fact that you panic tells me you probably don’t know much about what you own.

One important aspect of stock trading is not to get too complacent about the fact that they have smaller drawdowns than altcoins and feel 'safer'

Meaning, you can theoretically "average down" into a dip, but you have to:
1/ be very surgical about where you add (only on new local lows)
2/ de-risk on bounces
3/ know how many chips you have left so that you still have some if we reach an extreme drawdown (which would be 'deep value' to buy in the context of the LTF move)

It's also extremely easy to be buying a local top while feeling comfortable, without realizing you are actually at a very risky level for bulls

As usual, the main risk management lesson is all about one word: sizing.
Oversizing a trade is the main thing you should always try to avoid

thread_tweets.text:
ASE showcased its panel-level packaging (PLP) solution for AMD’s Venice CPU, with initial production targeted for Q1 2027, likely at limited scale at its Kaohsiung facility. ASE and its subsidiary SPIL have worked with AMD to implement the second generation of their Fan-Out Embedded Bridge (FOEB) technology in Venice. The current 310 × 310 mm panel accommodates 25 Venice interposers after edge loss, compared with 22 on a traditional round 300 mm carrier wafer, roughly a 14% increase in gross package count. This modest improvement in package output per carrier represents a starting point for panel-level interposers with Venice’s 2.7x reticle size, rather than evidence of a dramatic reduction in cost. (1/2)🧵
Source: OCP ASE Booth

ALERT🚨: The number of tokens that can be cached can increase by 20-40%🚀 by enabling DRAM KVCache offloading optimization at 12-16 concurrent agentic sessions. A B200 only has 180 GB of HBM, and after weight storage, only 100 GB of HBM per chip remains for KVCache.
